props.title: Rebecca
props.initialSlug: A bride haunted by her husband's first wife

sections.content: Alfred Hitchcock's Hollywood debut **Rebecca** (1940) masterfully adapts Daphne du Maurier's gothic romance with psychological terror and noir-tinged suspense. Producer David O. Selznick, fresh off **Gone with the Wind** (1939), gave Hitchcock considerable creative control, resulting in a haunting meditation on identity and power. Joan Fontaine's nameless second Mrs. de Winter, tormented by the ghostly presence of her husband's first wife Rebecca, showcases the director's fascination with vulnerable yet resilient heroines that would later emerge in **Vertigo** (1958) and **Marnie** (1964).

sections.content: The film established several Hitchcock signatures that would define his greatest works. The oppressive Manderley mansion prefigures the gothic architecture in **Psycho** (1960) and **The Birds** (1963), while Mrs. Danvers' sinister devotion to Rebecca's memory creates one of cinema's most memorable antagonists. Judith Anderson's portrayal influenced countless psychological thrillers, from **Whatever Happened to Baby Jane?** (1962) to **The Hand That Rocks the Cradle** (1992).

George Sanders brings sardonic menace as Rebecca's cousin Jack Favell, establishing a character type he would perfect in **All About Eve** (1950). The film's exploration of class anxiety and sexual repression influenced later gothic romances like **Dragonwyck** (1946) and **Jane Eyre** (1943), while its psychological complexity paved the way for **Gaslight** (1944) and **Secret Beyond the Door** (1947). sections.content: **Rebecca** sparked a wave of Hollywood gothic romances in the 1940s, including **The Spiral Staircase** (1946) and **The Ghost and Mrs. Muir** (1947). The film's influence extends to modern psychological thrillers like **Crimson Peak** (2015) and **The Others** (2001), which similarly blend romance with supernatural undertones. Cinematographer George Barnes' Oscar-winning black-and-white photography, particularly in the Manderley sequences, created a visual template for noir-tinged horror that resonates in films like **The Woman in Black** (2012).
